utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-32-T, the Prosecutor versus Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, I understand from one of the legal officers that you are concerned as to whether you are permitted to speak to your client during the United Nations holiday tomorrow. You understand that the general rule here is that once a witness starts to give evidence, his counsel cannot speak to him. The purpose of the rule is to overcome what was seen to be the practice, unfortunately, from the Prosecution side, of coaching the witness while they're giving their evidence. If you had finished his evidence-in-chief today and before he started his cross-examination, the Trial Chamber would consider giving you permission to speak to him. But if he's in the middle of either his evidence-in-chief or he's into his cross-examination, it would be unwise from his point of view because of inferences which could be drawn if he changes his evidence in any way. I'm not suggesting that there's going to be any impropriety, but it's just that the inference is open and it's wrong that your client should suffer if indeed it's a purely innocent discussion about the future conduct of the case. If you have finished your cross-examination before the end of today -- I'm sorry, if you finish your evidence-in-chief before the end of today, we would consider adjourning early so that the cross-examination can start on Thursday. We seem to have plenty of time in relation to only two witnesses this week. We'll hear what you want to say, Mr. Groome, about it later, but it seems to me if counsel are going off for what is now two weeks to prepare the case, it would be unfortunate if they were not able to take advantage of the UN holiday tomorrow, but obviously the timing of it will be important. Well, are you ready to start now, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, thank you. [Interpretation] The Defence of the accused Mitar Vasiljevic doesn't propose today to analyse the evidence that has been led by the Prosecution because we believe that it is appropriate to do so during the closing arguments of the Defence. We wish, Your Honour, during this opening statement merely to announce the evidence that we propose to lead, that is, the evidence to the fact which will prove that Mitar Vasiljevic did not commit the crimes with which he has been charged in the indictment. The witnesses of the Defence, including the accused Mitar Vasiljevic himself, will seek to prove that he was never a member of any paramilitary formation, neither a group belonging to -- neither the group belonging to Milan Lukic, nor did he ever use any weapon against anyone, nor did he participate in the planning or perpetration of the crimes with which he has been charged. Mitar Vasiljevic originates from a poor but honourable peasant family and, ever since his school days, he has been living of his own work, first as a waiter trainee, then as a waiter, and he was always a very good worker and liked by his colleagues and his guests, his clients. He started a family, he raised two children, and he began to build his family house. He was never involved in politics, neither prior nor during 1991 and 1992, the time when interethnic relations in the town of Visegrad got so exacerbated that numerous Serb families or individuals, as a minority, started abandoning the town of Visegrad either temporarily or for good. Mitar Vasiljevic continued with his life and his work there up until the month of May 1992, and he never had any differences with either Muslims or Serbs, nor did he enter into any kind of conflicts with either community. At one point in time he was mobilised into the Territorial Defence, and he took from his home the only military uniform which he had, the kind of uniform that other reservists had at the time; namely, a JNA uniform, a so-called SMB olive-drab uniform, so a unicoloured uniform. He was also issued with a weapon, and he started working in a military kitchen, in a canteen, in the village of Prelovo, which is located some ten kilometres from the town of Visegrad down the Drina River. The village is located at the same distance from his house which is situated on the outskirts of the town. We propose to call witnesses, Your Honour, who will testify to this particular fact, the witnesses who were with him in Prelovo, and who had also been mobilised to work in the military kitchen in Prelovo. They will testify that Mitar Vasiljevic was, throughout that period of time, with them in Prelovo, that he was working in the kitchen, that he was involved in procurement and maintenance of the kitchen, and that from time to time, whenever it was possible, he would go home to Visegrad where sometimes he would spend the night and then the next morning he would go back to Prelovo. Since he was never a driver - he never owned a driver's license or a car - on such occasions he would commute by hitchhiking and using vehicles that were passing by along the road or by covering some of the way on foot. And so it happened that on one particular night, in late May 1992, he was given a ride from the village of Prelovo to the town of Visegrad by Milan Lukic who, on that particular occasion, called in the village of Musici, a fact which was testified about by some Prosecution witnesses. And this is something that Mitar Vasiljevic will also testify about. Although the two families, the families Vasiljevic and Lukic, have had a very long relationship, more than 100 years old, a very close relationship, that of kumship, which means that they have many mutual godfathers and godmothers as well as best men and bridesmaids, which is a very old, very traditional Serbian - but not only Serbian - custom in that area. So despite that fact, Mitar Vasiljevic, up until that time, had almost not known Milan Lukic at all, because Milan belongs to a younger generation, a much younger generation than Mitar Vasiljevic; and furthermore, he was exiled from the area for a certain period of time and spent several years working and living in Switzerland, and also in the town of Obrenovac in Serbia. It was only at that period in time, that is, in the month of May 1992, that he came to the area of Visegrad together with his people from the town of Obrenovac in Serbia. Local residents of the town of Visegrad did not belong to his group, neither did Mitar Vasiljevic who, at that time, was a reservist serving in the military kitchen in Prelovo. Mitar Vasiljevic will testify, as will several other witnesses of the Defence, that he, Mitar, was even arrested at one point in time and detained in the prison in Uzamnica in late May 1992 or early June 1992, on which occasion he came to the Visegrad town on his own, on his own initiative, and went to his command at Bikavac to see Drago Gavrilovic. His intention was to return, again on his own, his weapon because he had refused to distribute food from the village of Prelovo to some positions which were not secured and where he was asked to go during the night. Because of this behaviour, because of this conduct of Mitar Vasiljevic, and also apparently because of the state of inebriation in which he was at the time he did this, he was arrested, he was taken into custody on the same day by the military police and detained in the prison in Uzamnica where he was visited and treated by witness Dr. Radomir Vasiljevic. It is very likely that Mitar Vasiljevic would have spent much longer time in that prison, longer than the three or four days that he spent there, if his cousin, his uncle's son, had not been killed, Sikiric Zeljko from the town of Vardiste, whom he loved very much. Following this incident, he went on a hunger strike and he asked to be released from prison to be able to attend the burial of his cousin. He was, therefore, released from prison and he started getting drunk very often, something that he hadn't been doing for quite some time because he had, prior to that, undergone treatment for alcoholism. Your Honour, we will call witnesses to testify about this, the witnesses who will also testify that on the day of the burial of his cousin, Zeljko Sikiric, he was completely drunk and totally beside himself and that it was impossible to establish any normal contact with him at that time. During those days, pursuant to a permission which was issued by his command, in order to avoid going to the military positions and to the former military unit which was located in the kitchen, he was tasked and he, indeed, began -- he was tasked with and began cleaning the streets of the town, including shop windows in business premises, from various kinds of debris and rubbish. It was for the purposes of this particular task that he assembled all of the local residents whom he was able to reach at that period of time, regardless of what ethnic community they belonged to. In those days, Your Honour, he wore a red ribbon tied around his sleeve, the same red ribbon which he used to wear earlier on in Prelovo. However, he no longer wore any military uniform nor did he carry any weapons. We will call witnesses to testify about this particular fact, the witnesses who knew him very well and who indeed used to be his neighbours. And that is how he happened to be, on the 14th of June, 1992, in the afternoon hours of that day, in the Pionirska Street. At the time, when coming from the direction of the centre of the town, a group of women, children, and elderly people arrived and found accommodation in the two houses belonging to the Memic families. At that moment, Mitar Vasiljevic was in the same street, however slightly further up the street, in the vicinity of the elementary school building. It was at that point in time that he came across a very good acquaintance of his, (redacted) (redacted), with whom he often used to go out and have a drink, and that is what he did on this occasion as well. He offered him some drink from the bottle that he was carrying and from which he had already been drinking. That particular conversation with (redacted) and the drink was everything in terms of contact that he had with that particular group of people, because this is -- it is because of this particular event that he was able to remember the events of the day. After that encounter, he continued further up the street to the spot where he found a horse which he rode all the way to the centre of the Visegrad town where, probably because of the slippery road conditions, because it was raining on that day, or perhaps because of the turn he did towards one of the witnesses who had called him, the horse fell down and Mitar consequently fell down as well. It was during that particular incident that Mitar Vasiljevic sustained a fracture on his left lower leg. This, Your Honour, will be testified about by witnesses, indeed, eyewitnesses who were present when Mitar Vasiljevic fell off the horse, the witnesses who assisted him before the arrival of the ambulance, which arrived upon somebody's invitation and whose driver, who will also be called to testify about these events, assisted by those who were present, again who will testify as witnesses, he carried Mitar into the ambulance and drove him to a physician on duty in the medical centre in Visegrad. The doctor examined him, sent him to have an x-ray taken, and ordered that he be transferred to the surgery ward to undergo medical surgery and further treatment in the hospital in Uzice. It was the same physician who ordered the driver to take him there as soon as it was possible. During that same afternoon, while it was still daylight, the driver, who was at that moment accompanied by the chief of accounting service of the medical centre, who will also be called to testify in this case, left in the ambulance for Uzice. Mitar was lying down in the ambulance and they started driving towards the town of Uzice, although the road was not safe enough because of very frequent ambushes but also because of very poor road conditions and weather conditions as well. During that journey, they stopped in the village of Vardiste which lies on the very road to Uzice in which village Mitar's uncle had a cafe. And the same witnesses will testify about this particular fact. They stayed there in that cafe for awhile. Mitar was given a blanket to cover himself because he did not leave the vehicle, he did not get out of the ambulance. So after that brief visit, they continued on their way to Uzice, arriving there sometime around 10.00 in the evening, and at that time, it was already dark. From information that we were able to obtain later on, the information which was obtained mainly from the hospital's register, which will also be presented as a Defence exhibit, we will be able to establish that the exact time of Mitar Vasiljevic's admittance into the hospital was 21 hours, 35 minutes of that day, that is, the 14th of June, 1992, although he had arrived sometime earlier than that. So he was admitted into hospital on the same day, x-rays were taken again, and he underwent surgery on the following morning. He spent three weeks immobile. And because of the crisis that he was undergoing due to his alcoholism and because of his behaviour in such a condition, after the weight extensions were taken off, he was transferred to the psychiatry ward where he spent, as an in-house patient, a certain period of time. He left the hospital on the 28th of July, 1992, the time when he was released from hospital on the explicit request made by his wife and not on the doctor's request. As regards this particular period of time, we intend to call certain witnesses who will also present numerous written and other material regarding his treatment. The Defence will show that he was admitted to hospital on the 14th of June, 1992 and that he spent that entire period of time in hospital, that is, until the end of the month of July 1992. We propose to call witnesses, Your Honour, to testify about these facts, the witnesses which will include members of the relevant hospital establishment, including physicians and nurses who participated in his treatment. Likewise, we intend to call witnesses who visited him while he was hospitalised or witnesses who happened to be in the same room as he was, as was the case of a man who had been seriously wounded and who is a Muslim national, of Muslim ethnic background, who was in hospital during that period of time having been admitted to that particular hospital on the 6th of May, 1992. That witness, Your Honour, will testify that Mitar Vasiljevic was indeed with him, that his behaviour was rather odd and strange, which was the main reason why he was transferred to the psychiatric ward for further treatment. Because of this behaviour of Mitar Vasiljevic and his delirious state due to alcoholism, evidence that he had undergone treatment for alcoholism before that, and his behaviour after his cousin died, and in view of all the available medical documentation and testimony of the physicians who treated him, and other medical personnel, we proposed a psychiatric expert witness who would examine the accused in order to establish his mental state and his accountability at the critical time, and an expert witness will testify to that. The period after Mitar Vasiljevic left the hospital is not covered by the indictment of Mitar Vasiljevic, the amended indictment, that is, and there was, therefore, no need for us to offer proof of his subsequent invalidity even if there is relevant medical documentation about that and even though there are witnesses who can also testify to these facts. On the basis of all the evidence produced, witness testimonies and evidence in writing, the Defence will show that there is not even a reasonable doubt [as interpreted] that Mitar Vasiljevic took, personally, part in the otherwise truly severe crime such as the murder of a large number of women, children, and elderly, caused by a fire in the night between the 14th and the 15th of June, 1992. He did not even know about this fire, nor could he even assume that anything like that could happen. With reference to the incident of the 7th of June, 1992, Mitar Vasiljevic is, unfortunately, the only witness for the Defence. At least, he was an eyewitness to this event and he offers a very logical and very persuasive explanation that he found himself at Vilina Vlas that day without a uniform and without any weapons as he did not have them any more at that time, and that he could -- he had no way of knowing or expecting that Milan Lukic and his group would also bring along a group of seven Muslim civilians whom, by all appearances, he wanted to leave there and then changed his mind and took them back in the same car whilst Mitar Vasiljevic, unfortunately, followed them, came along with them, believing that he was indeed taking them back and that they would give him a lift to his house as it was on their way. Regrettably, by all appearances, Milan Lukic has already devised a completely different plan, and rather than turning left towards Visegrad at a place called Sase, he took a right turn, heading for Prelovo, and shortly stopped the vehicles, and with two of his soldiers, took those men towards the Drina. Mitar Vasiljevic not only took no part in this, because, to begin with, he had no weapons, nor did this ever cross his mind, not to mention that he simply had no way of preventing Milan Lukic and his soldiers from doing what they were about to do. He was very distraught by this fact because, for the first time in his life, he witnessed killing, and in particular because one of the victims was his former and older colleague with whom he had always been on good terms. Following that, Mitar Vasiljevic was very depressed and continued to drink, which he had regrettably done before too and especially after his cousin's death which immediately preceded this incident. He then complained to his wife, who will also testify to these facts and other facts of relevance in this case, and he also complained to the then-chief of police, Tomic, who was the only man he trusted as Tomic had a reputation of a very honest man and policeman. However, by all appearances, he was also afraid to take any action whatsoever. And in addition to his already poor state of health, Mitar found that a sufficient reason to avoid any further encounter with Milan Lukic and his soldiers until his fall on the horse and injury on the 14th of June, 1992, after which date he was absent from Visegrad. These facts and the situation will be the subject of the defence. The Defence will try to show these facts by producing evidence and by having already produced some evidence and the witnesses it will call to testify about these facts and produced evidence in writing and findings of expert witnesses, the Defence expects that all of this evidence will show that there cannot be any reasonable doubt that the accused Mitar Vasiljevic, during the critical period of time, committed any of the crimes he's charged with between May and June of 1992, that he was never a member of Milan Lukic's paramilitary formation or any other formation, or that he committed any of the crimes for which he is accused. The Defence of Mitar Vasiljevic also proposes to begin its case by calling Mitar Vasiljevic as the first witness for the Defence before all the other evidence that the Defence will produce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. One particular thing I should raise at this stage: I don't know whether the accused's wife is in any position to hear the proceedings. If she is, she should now go away somewhere. She should not hear her husband's evidence before she gives her evidence. Secondly, just out of pure curiosity - and I hope you'll give some evidence about this - but can you explain to us what was the purpose of wearing this red ribbon? What did it signify?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I could gather from witnesses and Mitar himself, in Prelovo, all those who worked for the quartermaster, who worked in the army kitchen or were kitchen sweepers or something, had that red ribbon. That was sort of a mark to show that they were part of that unit. And he started wearing this ribbon again when he began to clean the town. At that time, he did not have any proper uniform or anything, so he wanted to wear it to show that he was responsible for the job. That is the only explanation, and I believe that Mitar himself and other witnesses will make the same kind of explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. One last thing: You said that there was an x-ray taken at the Visegrad medical centre. I notice that's not on the list of exhibits. I don't know whether this is something that you would like to pursue during your two-week break, but it is something which may or may not be very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think it will be very important if we could find any x-rays dating back to that time, bearing in mind, in the first place, that the x-ray which is in the record and which is part of the medical documentation and was turned over by the staff in Visegrad is questioned. So we really want very badly to find such an x-ray because that was done in Visegrad and in Uzice, of course. However, witnesses will testify about that. Under the then conditions, and generally in Yugoslavia, the practice was to give the x-rays to the patient himself so that he could take them and show them whenever he went for further checkups outside that particular institution. Mitar Vasiljevic did have some of these x-rays, perhaps not all of them, but unfortunately, these x-rays are no longer in his house, because when he was moving house he did away with very many things and presumably these same household documentation because he never thought he would need it again. We shall, nevertheless, try to find it, and if we succeed to do that in this fortnight that we have at our disposal, yes, I would be the happiest if we could find another x-ray.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: In any event, if you are unable to produce it, we would expect you to lead some evidence about the attempts or perhaps the provenance of the original x-rays and the attempts to find them. Now, are you ready to call your client? Thank you. Mr. Vasiljevic, will you come across to the witness box, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Stand up first, please, sir. Yes. Would you please make the solemn declaration in the document which the court usher is showing you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vasiljevic, I should first like to ask you to give us some particulars about yourself and your family. You were born in the village of Djurevac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And your father's name is?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Ljubisa.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And your mother?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Vojka.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel and witness please pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Both of you have been here long enough to know that there are problems with the interpretation if you answer straight away and if you ask the question straight away. So, Mr. Vasiljevic, please pause before you give your answer to enable the interpreters to catch up. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I was born on the 25th of August, 1954.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you have any brothers or sisters?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, I have one brother and three sisters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, can you tell us something about your education and how you learned your trade.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I graduated, I matriculated from a school of restaurant business, and I became a waiter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And where did you work?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I spent my career in a hostelry enterprise in Visegrad called Panos.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In other words, from your early days until the end, you worked always for one company only?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, I only worked for Panos. That was my only employer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And that company had a number of restaurants, of coffee bars, hotels, and so on, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Where did you work, or rather, did you work in different places, and for how long?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I started my career, I began -- my first job was in a spa, the former spa. Later on -- that is, I spent there some four or five years, I'm not sure. Then I moved over to Visegrad Hotel. Well, I practically worked at most of their facilities. Perhaps a couple -- there are a couple of coffee bars where I didn't, but Panos had a restaurant which was called after the company and that is in the centre of the town, and I worked there too. I worked at the restaurant called Usce, Brodar, Mezalin, and so on. I also worked in Pivnica, that is a brewery, and then we also had a restaurant called the Drina and I worked there too. There was a restaurant a Dobrun but I never worked there. And then we had another restaurant in the direction of Medzedza, I also worked there. There was a restaurant, or rather, a little coffee bar and I worked there too for awhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, I believe you mentioned that your first job was in Stara Banja, that is, old spa, Vilina Vlas, and the hotel that is often mentioned in this case, was that hotel part of your company, Panos, in 1992, or wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No, not in 1992, because they had split, some three years before that, into individual units, so that Panos and the old spa, Stara Banja, and the Vilina Vlas Hotel, was renamed the hotel and rehabilitation centre, recreation centre, Vilina Vlas. It was a kind of sanatorium.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So at that time, in 1992, it was a separate company, it was a company which became independent of Panos' company.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, no, it was a self-contained unit practically because we had our separate payroll and all the rest, and we were all part of Ehos company in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And in your company, the personnel must have included both Serbs and Muslims, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And on what kind of terms were you with those people; that is, did you -- were you at odds with any of them? Did you ever have any argument, any differences with them that would derive from your different ethnic origins?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No. The relations were very good. It had nothing to do with the ethnic composition. We all worked together and one never asked whom you were working with, whether it was Muslim or Croat or whoever. We did our jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did Meho Dzafic work with you?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Meho Dzafic worked with me for a very long time until his retirement. I think that in 1990 or 1991, perhaps a year or two before the war, he retired, and he was also my supervisor at the time when I was an apprentice under him and he was a very good tutor. He was an excellent waiter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you have any problems, did you ever fall out with him?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No, never. Meho Dzafic was very good to me, and I am in great debt to him because he was my tutor. Usually you underwent a two- or three-year apprenticeship. You work as a trainee, and then after you'd finished this, he often would invite me to his home. If it rained, if we worked long into the night, then he would invite me to spend the night at his place, or sometimes would -- he'd take the shift -- he'd take my shift so that I wouldn't have to stay there long, so on and so forth. And we worked there together for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you said that he was your supervisor, you mean he was a senior colleague of yours who trained you; you did not imply any kind of hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No, no. He was my teacher while I was an apprentice, while I was a trainee waiter. Once you complete your education, you become also what we call majstor, master, so it was in that sense that he was my teacher, and he was helping me as a junior waiter. At the time, I still had a lot of things to learn; how to manage to bar, how to serve people, and so on and so forth, because I did not have relevant experience, and he was there to impart his knowledge onto younger generations, including myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Both of you are forgetting that pause. Please remember. We want to hear all of your evidence, Mr. Vasiljevic, but we're going to lose some of it if you don't wait for a few seconds before you start your answer. So please remember that. I'm afraid, Mr. Domazet, you came in a few times there too. So just give us a pause.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, did you complete your compulsory military service with the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I did my military service, yes, in the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When, where, and in what section of the army you served?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I did my military service, that is, I completed my military service in late November 1973. Actually, it was the time I started my military service, and I was still in the military in 1994, up until mid-January 1995. The military service lasted 15 months, and I served in the town of Skopje, that is -- sorry, I apologise. I underwent training in Gorce Petrov, which is a town not far from Skopje, some ten kilometres away from the town of Skopje. It was a training centre. And after a four-and-a-half month course, I was transferred to the town of Stip, also in Macedonia, whereupon four of us cooks were transferred to work in the field, to the village called Leskovica, where we stayed until the end of our military service, working as cooks for force engineers, because force engineers unit was engaged on building a road there. So it was actually in the field that we did our military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said you were with the quartermaster service. Could you explain that to us? You said you were a cook. Does it mean that you worked in the kitchen, in the procurement, in similar services and that is what you did throughout your military service?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we were cooks. We prepared food. We worked in the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that you went -- that you began your military service in late November 1973; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At that time, the compulsory military service lasted how long?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Fifteen months. But I didn't serve 15 months because I did not use -- I did not avail myself of our regular leave, which was 20 days, and then I had some compensatory time off, so I managed to leave, to complete my military service earlier than usual. I was sent home earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But you completed your service sometime in January 1975?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, it was in mid-January that I left the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I've asked you this question again because I think you misspoke, and the transcript says that you completed your military service in 1995. Is that an error?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes. I finished my military service in 1975.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you start a family, Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I got married in February, 1988.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Where did you live after you got married?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: In Visegrad. And even prior to my marriage, I lived in Visegrad town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you live in the same house? Did you continue living in the same house?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, I continued living in the same house, which is actually our family house. But I was the only one living there at the time. I can provide you with the relevant details, if necessary. It was my father who bought the house, and I lived there. And since there was an agreement that I would build my own house, my father left the house to my brother, and it was agreed in the family that they would help me as much as they could to build my own house. And once I'm able to do that, that I would move to my new house, whereas the old family house would become the property of my brother. And it is still the property of my brother, but he never lived there. He works in Belgrade, and he's nine years younger than me. He found his first employment there and he never went back to Visegrad, so he never needed any accommodation in Visegrad, and that's why he never lived there, in that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you actually lived in the house which was bought by your father but which was intended for your brother, who at that time lived in Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I lived in that house from 1976, I believe; since it was bought. It was in 1976 that it was bought. Yes, 1976.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you had an agreement with your family according to which you would build your own house next to the family house, and once that house was completed, that you would move to this new house, leaving the family house to your brother?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So it was actually up until very recently that you were engaged in building that new house?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I spent a lot of time working on it. I was not in a hurry. I spent about 15 years working on it. But, you know, there was no need for me to hurry because I had accommodation. So I would work on the house whenever I had some spare time. And I personally never lived in this new house. My family now resides in that house. When I completed the house, when it became habitable, so to speak, I actually rented it out to members of the French SFOR contingent, so they were actually the first occupants of the house. And the house is located next to the old family house, some five or six metres away from it. So once again, I personally never lived in that house, but my family now resides in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So it was with the assistance of your father that you spent 15 years building that house, and the first occupants of the house were actually members of the French contingent of SFOR; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When did you actually rent it out, prior to your arrival here in The Hague? When was it exactly that you rented the house?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: It was on the 14th of July, I think, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So it would have been six months that those soldiers spent living in your house?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes. From the 5th -- until the 5th of January, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, when did you get married, and when were your children born?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I believe I already told you that I got married in February 1988. My first child, my daughter, was born -- actually, my first -- my very first child was a son but the baby died during the childbirth in 1989. And then I had a daughter on the 14th of July, 1980 [as interpreted], and then we had our third child, again a girl, who also died at childbirth. My wife had very severe problems with child-bearing, and eventually she had a Caesarean with her fourth child, a baby boy who was born in 1988 [as interpreted]. So that, thank God, I now have two children, a son and a daughter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, the dates, at least as interpreted, are a little strange. The first son -- first child was a son who died during the childbirth in 1989. That seems to be all right. Then your client is reported as having said he had a daughter on the 14th of July, 1980, and then there was the third child, no date is given, and then a baby boy who was born in 1988. Now, there seems to be some confusion either in the witness's mind or in the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. My first child, a boy, was born in 1979, not in 1989, because my daughter was born in 1980, the second child. Sorry, I was wrong ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, were you also wrong about the date of your marriage? Because the transcript said that you got married in 1988.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I'm sorry, I apologise; in 1978, when I got married. Yes, 1978.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think we're straight now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, I should like to ask you now about something that turned out to be quite significant in this case, and that is the relationship of kumship between your family and the Lukic family which originates from the village of Rujiste. Would you please explain to the Court how long have your two families been related in this particular manner, and in what way has this relationship been sustained all these years?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I cannot give you the exact details as to when we first established this relationship of kumship. I don't think my father or my grandfather would know about it. It is not only our particular Vasiljevic family that is in this particular relationship with the Lukic family; it extends further on to all of the Vasiljevic families from my village. All of our families have this very close link with the Lukic family from Rujiste. We exchanged godfathers, godmothers, best men at weddings, and so on and so forth. So all of the Vasiljevic families have been in this type of relationship with the Lukic family for a very, very long time. As to where it all began, I really couldn't tell you, I just know that it is a very long-standing tradition within our two families.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, it extends beyond the generation of your grandfather. So can we agree on the fact that this particular relationship has been going on for more than a hundred years between your two families?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And likewise, if I understand you correctly, this relationship concerns and involves all other families originating from the old Vasiljevic and Lukic families from the village of Djurevici and Rujiste respectively, regardless of their subsequent places of residence?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So Milan Lukic is also from one of these Lukic families with whom your family, the Vasiljevic family, was closely related?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes. My father was his godfather and he was also his sister's and brother's godfather. And maybe even my grandfather, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, how well did you know Milan Lukic personally before the month of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I knew Milan Lukic as a student while he was attending school in Visegrad, and I also knew him when he was a child. And then I know that, when he completed his secondary school, he went off to the army to do his military service, after which he left for Switzerland and I no longer saw him until 1992. Well, as to how well I knew him as a person, that is a different matter. He is, I believe, 13 years younger than me, and we never socialised together. We didn't belong to the same generation, and so I can't say I knew him very well. And then he was not living in Visegrad, he was in Switzerland.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So after he finished his secondary school and completed his military service, he left the area of Visegrad; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: He worked in Switzerland. Do you know his place of residence at that period of time, since everybody worked abroad needed to have an official place of residence abroad? Was his official place of residence still in Visegrad or was it abroad?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I'm not sure I quite understand you. What do you mean, that he lived in Visegrad and worked in Switzerland? I apologise. I don't think I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Mr. Vasiljevic, I was not referring to his formal, official whereabouts, though if you know that, you can tell us that, of course. I would like to know where in Yugoslavia he was registered as a resident while he was working in Switzerland. Was he a resident of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I think his place of residence, officially speaking, was in Belgrade, that he bought an apartment in Belgrade at the time he was working in Switzerland.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The town of Obrenovac has been frequently mentioned in this case. Is that town in any way related or connected with Milan Lukic or not?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Whether prior to his departure for Switzerland he had worked in Obrenovac, I don't know. All I know, that his brother used to work in Obrenovac as a teacher. Whether Milan worked there as well, I don't know. Even if he did, that could have only been prior to his departure for Switzerland, if he did work there. Obrenovac is not very far from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The Lukic family is a very large family; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you answer my previous question, was your response that Milan Lukic was officially residing in Belgrade at the time he was working in Switzerland, that is to say that he was no longer officially a resident of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he has an apartment in Belgrade, that is correct, at the Bezanijska Kosa neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: During that period of time, that is, several years before the events in May 1992, did you ever happen to see him in person?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Before or after May? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Before the month of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No. Especially the last year or two, no. No, I don't remember -- I don't remember seeing him during those five years, perhaps. No, no, I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm about to cover one portion -- actually, I have covered this subject matter, and I think this is the convenient time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, let's turn to you and the state of your health. We have heard here about certain injuries that you sustained, and fractures. You broke your leg in 1992, on the 14th of June, as you rode a horse; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And before that, did you ever sustain a similar injury; that is, did you break your leg on any other occasion prior to that?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No, never. Never leg or arm or anything, not even a finger.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And after that, after 1992?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I broke my leg in 1992 and then I broke the same left leg in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And in which hospitals did you receive treatment on those two occasions?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Both these fractures were treated at the Uzice hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were you ever hospitalised in the Uzice hospital at any other time and on any other occasion?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: In 1976, I was hospitalised there because I had trouble with my lymph nodes, and I spent there two months, and then I was transferred to Sarajevo to the hospital called Pod Hrastovima, under the oaks. And in 1980-something, four or something, I was again in hospital receiving treatment for alcoholism. I think I was in the Uzice neuropsychiatric ward on three different occasions. And that thing in 1992 was, I think, my fourth time in the neuropsychiatric ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So on these three occasions prior to 1992, were you then on all those three occasions hospitalised for alcoholism?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We did not hear the answer. We are sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You better ask the question again. There was no answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you mention three times when you were admitted to hospital in Uzice prior to 1992, were you hospitalised on all these three occasions for alcoholism?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I said in 1976 was the first time that I was in the hospital, to treat my lymph nodes, and then, yes, I was admitted to the hospital three Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. times to receive treatment for alcoholism, and that was when I was at the neuropsychiatric ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Apart from the treatment in hospital, were you also treated as an outpatient

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you tell us, Mr. Vasiljevic, something about your reactions when you are under the influence or drunk. What can you tell us about how you behave under those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, if I start drinking, it is difficult for me to give up. I crave for alcohol. So that - I don't know how to put it - if I'm not too deep into it and if I go to the outpatient clinic for infusion in time and start eating, then I manage to pull myself away. I was an addict, really. I mean, if I got to drinking, it was very difficult for myself to pull myself away, although -- and I couldn't eat. I simply craved for alcohol.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And in such situations and when you were in such a state, were you aggressive?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No. I liked to have company when drinking. I liked to drink, I mean, I liked to drink. It didn't matter who it was with. If I had -- I was capable of spending all the money I had on me, and everybody around me drank when I drank. People knew me in the -- around town and people felt sorry for me, my colleagues reproached me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But my question was specifically what do you think, were you aggressive on such occasions towards people around you?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No, no, no. I was -- I simply liked to drink. I didn't quarrel with anyone if someone provoked me. At times, I could even work. Well, not when I was really drunk, but I could even work. I would just go behind the bar and have a couple and -- well, I couldn't, of course, work when I was stone drunk, when I was stoned, but otherwise I could drink and work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When I asked you if you were aggressive, I mean physical aggression --

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Please wait for my question. But in such situations, did you ever attack anyone around you or --

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No, no, no, never. Never. I never. I liked to sing and drink, and that -- no, no, I never offended anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did it ever happen, then, that in such situations, when in such a state, you would start talking uncontrolled, perhaps start talking, whatever, and then insult, even unwittingly, anyone?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, in the beginning, when I was younger, even when I was sloshed, I knew perfectly well who I was with, how I was, what coffee bar or what, whether I'd walked home or been driven to it. Later on, I stopped being aware of those things, and quite often I wouldn't know who I'd been with and who had brought me home. Who knows all that went on and how it went on; I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, when you say when you were younger that you could take drink better, that you still remember events, and that later on you stopped remembering these things, but do you ever recall if, when under influence, when you were very young, do you remember committing any offence, any crime, for which you were imprisoned then? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And was that offence the singing of an offensive song in the company of other persons who were also brought to justice together with you?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: How old were you then, Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I was 18, 18 -- 18 and 11 months, thereabouts, or 18 and 10 months. I was 18 and 10 months old.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Right. But under Yugoslav law, it means you were of age already and you were tried and sentenced and you served your term, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was that the only time that you served a term in prison?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vasiljevic, I'd like to move on to another topic, and that is Visegrad on the eve of the arrival of the Uzice Corps, in other words, early April 1992. Can you tell me, but concisely, what you were doing then, and in briefest possible terms, what went on in Visegrad at the time.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, what do you want me to tell you? Before the Uzice Corps, there were some -- I don't know where to begin. I think that the police split up into the Muslim and Serb police. They stopped working together. Whether all of them or not, I don't know. So that this tension rose. And sometime around the 10th or 11th, I was at home at the time, and there was a threat that the whole power plant would be blown up, and I heard this conversation on the radio. And people panicked. Nobody believed that that might happen. But some of the gates were opened and water -- but if it happened, then water started to pour in. I don't know whether there were any people in the town, Serbs or Muslims, but I know that we withdrew to the village called Omar. And the Serb policemen were captured at the time, some of the regular force and some of these - what you call it - the reserve force, and they were taken up to the hydro power plant or something. I can't tell you every little detail, but all I know is that they were captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, did this make people leave the town, I mean, both the Muslim and the Serb inhabitants, were they prompted to leave the town?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, I didn't go into town to tell you whether they'd all left, but yes, most people did, Muslims and Serbs, as likely as not, because when water was released, nobody could be happy about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So if I understand you well, Mr. Vasiljevic, before that happened, you had already left Visegrad and you were somewhere in the vicinity. When you say Kalate, is Kalate the name of the locality where your house in Visegrad is?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And how far was that from your house, that is, the town itself?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: You mean where we went to, where we went from Kalate?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, it's not far. It's a hill of 500 or 600 metres, the village of Omar. But it wasn't safe there. Serbs were arriving from the town on the run too, so that we moved on to Banja, to the spa, which is some three kilometres further away, the village of Jelasica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And why wasn't it safe, as you say? Can you explain it? How wasn't it safe?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, these Serb policemen were captured, and people fled up towards the border with Serbia, so that we all had to fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You say people fled towards the boundary with Serbia. What people do you have in mind, Mr. Vasiljevic? Do you mean the Serb or the Muslim population, or both?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Serb, by and large, but there were also some Muslims who were fleeing to Serbia. I know that up at the sanatorium, there were Serbs and Muslims, and that we transferred all the patients there to the boundary as we went, as we were on our way. They were all heading towards the boundary.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And in that village, in the village of Jelasica where you were, were you there when the Uzice Corps arrived in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes. We heard that the Uzice Corps had arrived whilst we were up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: From what you could hear or learn personally, did the arrival of the Uzice Corps help to improve the situation, to calm down the situation, in Visegrad and around it, or was it the other way around?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, when they came, the situation became more normal. There was no more tension. They invited all the population, Serb and Muslim, to go back to work. And then, well ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And did people go back to work and to the town itself?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And you, Mr. Vasiljevic, do you have any recollection of any incident at that time, any note-worthy incident during that time while the Uzice Corps was still in the town?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Before the Uzice Corps came, yes. The first victim was, I believe, a Serb. He could have been around 25 or so, Mico Indzic, and I think he was the first victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, but you are talking about the time before the Uzice Corps arrived and you yourself said that there was tension in Visegrad. But my question was while the Uzice Corps was there, were there any serious incidents then in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if there were any serious incidents. I did not hear anything about any serious incidents. They had their commanders. They were the army. The army was under the command. There could have been a victim or two. I know there was some Smajic and his wife, but I don't know how that came about. Medo Smajic, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, did these soldiers of the Uzice Corps have their checkpoints on the roads, and if yes, was one such checkpoint near your house?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes. They had their checkpoints usually, as a rule, on bridges, then at junctions, at the intersections, and one was near my house, that is, towards the village of Omar. That was one such crossroads. And they manned it for some ten days or so, when that checkpoint was moved to the village of Sase.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your street, the street on which your house is, is called Vojvode Stepe; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And is it on the main road, or perhaps the only road leading from the centre of Visegrad to Sase, that is, Vilina Vlas, and Prelovo which is still further away, that is the only road there?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: If you go by car. If you go on foot, you can cut across the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Speaking of the checkpoint which was located in the vicinity of your house, on the road, that is, in your street, did you, at any point in time during that period, have any specific tasks such as duty shift? Were you in charge of controlling people passing through that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No. It was impossible for us to participate in their duties. They had their own army, their own command. They did not ask us to do any such tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, could you now describe for us what happened with you specifically after the departure of the Uzice Corps.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: After the Uzice Corps had left, I received call-up papers for mobilisation. I was asked to report at the school in Prelovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you respond to the call-up papers that you received?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At that time, did you have a uniform belonging to the reservists of the JNA at house [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And did you take that uniform with you when you went to Prelovo?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you please describe for us what kind of uniform it was.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: It was a former JNA uniform, the so-called SMB uniform. I was issued that uniform some ten years prior to the events. That kind of uniform was issued to all of us, Muslims, Serbs, Yugoslavs. It was in the former Yugoslavia, and it was the kind of uniform that we kept at home, we members of the reserve forces. Usually, once you were over 30, you would become a member of the reservists, of the reserve force of the army. So I had that uniform for about ten years, and it was a regular olive-drab uniform. I was not the only one. All of us had this kind of uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would it be correct for me to say that all members of the reserve force had such a uniform at home, and that that was the kind of uniform that they would take when they were called to perform military exercises?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say that all of us had such uniforms, but the majority of us did. Some people maybe didn't have it; maybe they received it later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you said that it was an olive-drab uniform of the former JNA, did you mean that it was a unicoloured uniform which was olive-grey in colour, a rather light hue of olive-grey?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it had only one colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you tell us something more about the unit to which you were sent in Prelovo.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: It was a quartermaster unit. It belonged to the quartermaster department.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What does that mean, Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I was assigned to that particular unit together with another cook. We had an assistant as well and a driver, and there was also a paramedic with us, a male nurse. So that would have been, what, five of us altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember any of the names of those people, Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I know all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you please tell us the names you remember.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: The chief cook was an elderly man who, prior to that, used to work in various canteens and restaurants in Serbia. Whether he was retired or not, I don't know. But his name was Vaso Vojnovic. The driver was a relative of his who used to work in Visegrad as a driver for the forestry company, and his name was Obren Vojnovic. The assistant was Dragisa Lindo, and the paramedic, Stevo Grujic, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember anyone else who was there but not a member of your unit?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I know that Dragan Simic was there, the commander Krsto Papic, because the command was there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So, Mr. Vasiljevic, could you give us a description of your personal duties during your time in Prelovo.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: When I arrived in Prelovo, we were immediately assigned to various tasks. The main cook, the chief cook, as I said, was Vaso Vojnovic. And I was tasked with procurement of foodstuffs and kitchenware, because it was at the very beginning, so I was also supposed to help with the kitchen work whenever I was there. So that is how we began our work at the school there. But we had some difficulties with cooking there so we moved to another building, to a house nearby, in order to be separate from the rest of the troops. So we prepared food there. My duty was to take food to the front line, together with the driver, Obren Vojnovic, so this is what we did. We would drive the food to the front line, which at the time was in the village of Blace. We distributed lunch, and in the evening, dinner, except on the occasions when they only had a can of food or a sandwich for dinner, something not cooked. In general, then that would be distributed together with the lunch so that we didn't have to go again in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The distribution of food to the front lines, in your opinion, was it dangerous for you during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes. I personally was scared, especially during the night. During the day, it was more or less okay, I wasn't that afraid. However, during the night, I had problems doing it. It was really difficult for me to do that, but I had to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you complain about that problem to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I omitted to ask you at the beginning of this Prelovo section whether you were issued any weapon.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We believe the witness said yes.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I was issued with an automatic rifle, some machine-gun called Schmeisser, before I left for Prelovo. So when I got to Prelovo, I returned that weapon and was issued instead an automatic rifle; that is, I returned the Schmeisser or the sub-machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So that was the rifle that you carried with you at the time you were in Prelovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you ever go to Visegrad, either on business or for other reasons, during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes. I would usually go to Visegrad in the morning to obtain the necessary things, and sometimes I would even go twice a day if I needed to bring some kitchenware, some pots and pans, if necessary, if there were things that needed to be brought to the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You have told us that you personally never drove a car, neither did you have a driver's license. Who was it who took you there?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Obren Vojnovic did, in a van.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That would have been your official journeys from Prelovo and back for the purposes of the kitchen you were working for?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you ever leave Prelovo to go to your house? Did you stay at your house for awhile and then return to the unit?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes. If I was able to find some transport, I was allowed to go home until the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, whenever it was possible for you to do that, in view of the duties that you had at Prelovo, and whenever you were able to find some transport, you would go home in the evening and then come back on the following day?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, except that we were not allowed to use the van for our personal purposes, only for the kitchen. But we personally were not allowed to use it for our needs, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So on those other occasions, how did you go home?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, usually, I would stop a car passing by. Someone would give me a lift.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, do you remember one particular occasion during that period of time being driven from Prelovo to your home by Milan Lukic, personally? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Court when that was and whether you made a stop on the way.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: It was sometime in late May. I was standing by the road, waiting for someone to pass by, and Milan Lukic, together with two other vehicles coming from the direction of Prelovo, passed by, so I stopped them and asked them to give me a lift to Visegrad. As we were getting near the village of Musici, which lies some three or four kilometres away from Prelovo, he said he had to stop to check if anyone had any weapons there, because allegedly someone had opened fire on the police patrol. And I said, "Milan, why do you want to have anything to do with them? I mean, you were not shot at." But he stopped in that village, and others got out as well, and they went towards the [redacted] house, and I said, "Milan, for God's sake, please don't touch those people." I knew all of them. Perhaps not personally, but I did know them. But he entered their house and he asked if anyone had any weapons. To tell you the truth, I was aware of the fact that both [redacted] 24 [redacted] were members of the [redacted], but I never told him that. I didn't want to tell him that. It wasn't my intention to say anything. I know for a fact that both [redacted] were members of the [redacted], but I never told him that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just one moment, sir. What's the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: He's referring to protected witnesses. If I might, I've prepared a pseudonym sheet for cross-examination. I would offer it to Defence, if they care to use it, and he can refer to them by their pseudonyms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That might be a very good idea, Mr. Domazet. Have you got a copy of it for us so that the redactions can be made?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have you ascribed a number for it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just a second, Your Honour. While we're discussing this, I might also state that in the accused's interview in November, he expressed concern that two names would be mentioned, that it could cause possible harm to his family. I would have no objection if the Court assigned them Defence pseudonyms. I will be asking him about those two gentlemen, and their names are on the bottom of that sheet. The next number would be Prosecution document number 164, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P164, and it's under seal. In relation to Defence pseudonyms, have you thought of any numbers? We've used VGD-1 and VGD-2. But have you organised any others, Mr. Domazet, or shall we just proceed with 3 and 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour, that we continue with numbers 3 and 4, because I still don't have a separate list so I don't think there's any problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, the first of the additional names on Exhibit P164 should be referred to as VGD-3, and the second of those names as VGD-4. Perhaps they better be written on the sheet that the witness has so that he's got them readily available to him. I interrupted the answer, I'm sorry. Can you pick it up, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome, for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, before we continue, I should like to ask you to have a look at this list, and should it become necessary for you to mention any of these individuals, to indicate them by number instead of using their names. As regards the two last individuals on the list, you have separate numbers if we should have any questions in relation to them.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours, for having mentioned the name of Witness 059. So when he got to their house, he entered the house. I was standing in front of the door --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, would you please wait for my question first. Mr. Vasiljevic, try to concentrate on my questions and give me specific and brief answers to them. First of all, do you remember how many vehicles there were in addition to Milan Lukic's car with whom you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. drove?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Three. I believe that there were three vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did Milan Lukic's car stop some 20 metres away from the house of Witness VG-059?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Where did the other vehicles stop?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I think they stopped somewhere in the vicinity. It's a small village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The individuals who were in those other vehicles, were they wearing a uniform and carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I could tell. I don't know whether all of them were. I don't know. I mean, I didn't know all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What kind of uniforms did they have, including Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Most of them were wearing camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did Milan Lukic also have a uniform like that?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were you wearing your uniform, the one that you had when you were in Prelovo?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: You mean the SMB uniform?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Did you have it on on that evening?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, most probably -- yes, I did. I don't know what else I would have had on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you also have your weapon, the one you were issued whilst in Prelovo?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: A moment ago you told us that it was only Milan Lukic who entered the house of VG-059.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And you only reached the door and stood in the doorway. That is how you explained it to us.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you see where other soldiers went?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, they were there in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell us if Milan Lukic said something or if he asked something from those people whose house he had entered, briefly?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Weapons only.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say "weapons only," does that mean that he asked them if they had any weapons, or something else?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: If anyone had any weapons and if they knew who had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And what did they answer?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Nothing. They said they had nothing. And people from the village gathered. He was with them there. What they talked about word for word, I cannot say. But he was looking for weapons, saying, "Does anyone have any weapons? If yes, turn it over," things of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Let's move slowly, Mr. Vasiljevic. If I understood you well, at first Milan Lukic was alone with the members of the family of the witness 059, and then you say other people gathered. Does that mean that other villagers had come to that house?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: The house that he entered belonged to the father of Witness 059, and his brother was there too, and 59 too, 55 was there, the wife of 59, but they came later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understood you well, you said that a little later some other villagers of Musici also turned up; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And did Milan Lukic say to them the same thing about weapons, or perhaps did he ask something else?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And during that time while you were there, were there any incidents or did anything happen that would indicate that there was something between them?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: In the house belonging to the father of 059, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you then leave the village of Musici altogether and head for Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I asked and gave my word to Milan that those people were good people, because I went to school with the brother of 059, and he wanted to go and search. And I gave him my word that he was telling the truth, that there was nobody up there. And Witness 59 said so in his statement to the investigators. I trusted those people, I said. And that day, there was nothing; he didn't rob them or hit anyone, he didn't.
