utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understand what you are saying, nobody searched the houses, nobody went to the attic or --

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No, no, no, not the attic. Just the rooms and kitchen, I think, but not the attic. I said I know, the many questions said to me, there is nothing and I said so because I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And after that, did you leave Musici altogether? I mean, the same vehicles, you in the car that you had come up in and the others in their cars?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, I left with them, I think all of them. I got off where my house is because it's slightly in front of Visegrad, slightly before you enter Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So with them, you reached your house which is at the entrance into Visegrad, on the same road, and that is where you parted company with them.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I got off when we reached my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And after that, did you ever go to the village of Musici again with Milan Lukic or anyone else from his group?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No, never again did I go there with Milan Lukic, to the village of Musici, and I'm quite positive about that. I did go through the village, though, because that's the only road which takes one to Prelovo. But not with Milan Lukic, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And did your unit, that army kitchen at Prelovo, did it receive orders to relocate to the village of Blace, or in its direction?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I asked to be transferred to the village of Blace to avoid commuting by night, but they would not allow it. And later on it turned out that I had been in the right, and then they did transfer me. Perhaps we do not understand one another. We took the food to the village of Blace, and the army kitchen was moved over there later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understand you well, at the time when the kitchen was relocated to the village of Blace, you were no longer with it?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No, no, no. It was transferred to the village of Blace while I was still in Prelovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Will you tell us, how did it come about that you stopped being in Prelovo, rather, in that army kitchen?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: The line from Prelovo to the village of Blace where we took food was to be moved five kilometres on to the village of Rujiste and the village of Paocici which is below the village of Rujiste. The road takes you through the forest there. And I refused to take the food there at night, and they then returned to Visegrad and gave me a reference so that I would report to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So where did you go, and what happened then?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I went to Bikavac where the command was, reported to Drago Gavrilovic, and he says to me that I have to go back and I tell him that I won't. There was no way that I could take any food anywhere at night, especially now that the front line was being moved another five kilometres. "You have to do it." "I can't, I daren't, I won't." "Well, drink less and then you'll dare," he says. To tell you honest, without a drink, I would never move from my house, I would be afraid to do that. So we did not manage to see eye to eye. I returned the weapon -- no, I forgot to say, I didn't -- when I had started from Prelovo, up there they took away my automatic rifle and gave me back the submachine-gun, the one that I had been issued with before. At Bikavac, I returned the submachine-gun, and Drago says, "Mitar, you're going to be put behind the bars." I said, "It's all right with me. I don't care. I am too afraid to go there," and that's the end of it. And they did arrest me that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, do you remember the day when that happened or the period of time when that happened?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I think it was the 29th. They did not give me any disposition or decision or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you think it was the end of May 1992; is that it? When you say that you were arrested the same day, was it at that same place or where?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: It was down in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And who arrested you?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Two military policemen. Let me tell you, they invited me to board their car. They did not try to do anything to me; they did not use any force. "Come along, get into the car." I did. They took me to the station. They were quite correct. I didn't expect that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But he gave you -- they gave you no paper, no document about it at all?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No. I asked for it and they promised. They said allegedly I'd spent 15 days in gaol.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And where did they take you?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: To the Uzamnica -- to Uzamnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was that a prison or what?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: It was the barracks. Earlier, I mean, it was the JNA barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the people who worked there or who were possibly serving terms at the same time?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: When I arrived up there, I found there another prisoner, Pero Simcic his name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And that Pero Simcic was incarcerated in the same place, in the same room?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, we were in the same room.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And do you remember any of the staff of that prison?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, there was a colleague of mine who distributed food there. There were guards too.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I did not catch the name of the man who distributed food.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The interpreters lost the name there, if he gave one. Mr. Vasiljevic, you do drop your voice quite often. Just remember that it's got to get through to the interpreters. Indeed, it's got to get through to Mr. Domazet as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Will you please repeat the name of that man who you say is your colleague and served food there.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Ilija Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. And during the term, did you receive any medical attention?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Whose?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Dr. Vasiljevic, and a nurse who came with him. I think her name, her first name is Marica. I don't know what her last name is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And why did that doctor and that nurse come to see you?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: My nerves were in a bad state. I suppose alcohol had something to do with it. So he gave me an infusion. I was on a hunger strike.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember how, at the time when you were arrested and taken to Uzamnica, if you were drunk then?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, yes, to be quite frank, I never stopped drinking at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was that the reason or one of the reasons for the intervention by the doctor and the nurse?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember, how many days did you spend at Uzamnica?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, I was released from Uzamnica after my cousin was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Which cousin, Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Zeljko Sikiric.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And where was he killed; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Up there somewhere near Brodar, in the direction of Medzedza. Somewhere in the woods. I don't know exactly where, but it was near Brodar somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You say that was the reason why they let you out of the prison. After how many days; can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I spent three days up there. Three or maybe four.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And did you attend the funeral of your cousin Sikiric?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did this funeral take place only, more or less, immediately after he died, or did it take place a few days later; do you remember that? Or let me rephrase this. Funerals usually take place a day or two after the demise. That is a custom with us. Was that the case in this particular instance?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No, because they were killed in the woods. There were two neighbours with him, and these other two were -- got out before him and they were buried a couple of days before him. So one had to wait, I don't know how long really, while they found them and then could get to them. They had to wait for the army to liberate it. So that he wasn't brought that same day, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So from the moment when your cousin was killed until the time when his body was pulled out and then buried, several days elapsed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you explain the relationship? Who is he? What is he?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: He's my uncle's son. Dobrivoje Sikiric.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So Dobrivoje Sikiric is your mother's brother; is that it?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Where did he live?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: In the village called Vardiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And Vardiste is on the main road from Visegrad to Uzice; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At that time, did he have a coffee bar in that village?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: He did. He must have had it for some ten years at the time, perhaps even longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, did you attend Zeljko Sikiric's funeral?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you -- if you can remember, that is, were you under influence at that time or not?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Why? Could you explain it, please?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, I was sorry; we were relatives. I grieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'll move on to another matter, and that is the 7th of June, 1992 and what happened that day. Let me remind you. It was the incident with which you are charged. Do you remember what you did that day, and how did it happen that you went to Vilina Vlas?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: When they released me from Uzamnica, from prison, I reported to the command and begged them not to lock me up again. And then they let me organise the cleaning of the town. And that day I was on my way back home, and before I got there, Stanko Pecikoza in a car caught up with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And who was Stanko Pecikoza?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Stanko Pecikoza was a Serb from Vise, a businessman. He had his sawmill and his carpenter shop about a kilometre from my house, in a village called Kosovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is this convenient, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: How are you going for your estimate and the length of your evidence-in-chief? I have in mind your wish to speak to the witness tomorrow. Do you think you'll be finished by 4.00?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I hope to finish before then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't want you to hurry it in any way, but it certainly would be to yours and the accused's advantage if you do finish by 4.00. But please don't feel in any way pushed. We'll adjourn now until 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, we left off at the moment when you started talking about Stanko Pecikoza and his encounter with yourself on the 7th of June. I should like you to continue describing that particular encounter. On that day, Stanko Pecikoza stopped his car and then you saw him, and can you please tell us what happened next.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes. Stanko stopped his car and he asked me whether I knew where Lukic was, whether I had seem him around. I said, "Stanko, I don't know. It's possible that he's at Banja, because that's where he usually spends the night." And then he asked me whether I would like to join him, to go to Banja, and I said, "Yes, why not," because it was an opportunity for me to take my waiter's uniform which was left over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your waiter's uniform was there for how long?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, I left it there at the time I worked there at Banja, while the Uzice Corps was there, while I worked there. But not all the time, maybe for about 15 days. So that is how we set out towards Banja.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just a moment. Does that mean, Mr. Vasiljevic, that you had not been at Banja ever since, that is, since the time you left your waiter's uniform there?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, I did go to Stara Banja once or twice while the locality was still functioning, while the corps was there. But no, I didn't go there very often, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So did you go to Vilina Vlas with Stanko Pecikoza in his car?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you see anyone there when you got there?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Milivoje Susnjar was at the reception desk and I asked him whether he knew about Milan Stanko, because they were looking for him because of the incidents that he was involved in. Stanko was active in the party. I don't know exactly what he was, he was a deputy chairman, I think. And he was very much against Milan and his behaviour, his actions. But anyway, he wasn't there, and Stanko told me to -- well, he actually asked me to stay there and he said, "If he should come back, please let me know that he's there, and I'm now going to look for him, see if I can find him." He said, "I'm going down to Prelovo to see if he's there," because he had already been looking for him for quite some time, around the town mostly. So Stanko left and I remained there with Milivoje for awhile. I was not able to get my uniform, my waiter's uniform, because the area behind the kitchen was locked up, and that is where our cloakrooms were. So I was unable to get there. But I stayed there for awhile, half an hour maybe, and then Milan Lukic came, together with seven Muslims and three or four other people with him whom they had collected in Bikavac. Meho Dzafic was there and his son.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I should like you to pause for awhile. Could you please focus on my question so that we can give the Court as precise a description as possible. So you remained at Vilina Vlas, and Milivoje Susnjar was the only individual who was with you at the time. Milivoje Susnjar is the one whom you found when you got there.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Some 30 minutes after Pecikoza left, Milan Lukic came with his men, taking with him a group of people amongst whom you recognised Meho Dzafic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Objection. Leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think it was a leading question. If it's important, Mr. Domazet, you really should not lead because it destroys the value of his answer. If you want to object, let's hear you say it. I can't look at both sides of the courtroom at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mitar Vasiljevic himself said that seven Muslims arrived with him, including Meho Dzafic and his son, and that was the reason why I phrased my question the way I phrased it, because he had already given me the answer. However, I will try to rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If he had, it was some time ago, because I don't recall it, frankly. But if he had said it, then it was not a leading question. But let's not argue, let's get on with the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The individuals whom you just mentioned entered the hotel. Where were you at that moment?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: At the reception desk of the hotel. Actually, I was not inside, I was in front of the reception. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In that lobby, there is a door on the left leading to the swimming pool, then a cloakroom, and then further down the hall is the reception. Can you remember exactly where you were at the moment those people entered the building?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, I was there near the desk. I mean, I was around. I was in the lobby, right in front of the reception desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were you armed?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At the time, were you issued with any weapon at all?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No, I was not. I told you that I had returned my weapon when I was captured, when I was arrested, at Bikavac. It was at Bikavac that I returned my weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you have your uniform on?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What kind of uniform? Could you describe it for us, please.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: The usual SMB uniform; the trousers, T-shirt, a shirt, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The trousers were part of the SMB uniform. What about the shirt? Was it a military shirt or a civilian shirt?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Most probably it was also an SMB shirt, a sports shirt or a similar one. I don't know. I changed shirts very often in those days because I was cleaning the town, so I probably had this kind of a sports shirt on at that time as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you have anything on your head?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I had a hat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What kind of hat, Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: A black hat which was usually worn by the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you often wear this hat?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Sometimes, though not always.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: On that particular occasion, did you have a red ribbon tied around your sleeve?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Why did you wear that ribbon? Could you explain that to us, please.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: It was a kind of sign, indicating that I was working as a cleaner, that I had my duty in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you now tell us what happened when this group of people entered the hotel, when they came to the reception? Did any one of them speak to Susnjar, who was the only person present there, and what happened next?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Susnjar was working at the reception. He was a kind of janitor there. He had been one even prior to the war. So when Milan and his men entered together with those Muslims, he went to look for the keys. Actually, Milan asked for the keys but Susnjar didn't want to give him the keys because he was very rude, Milan, that is, and he was persistent. He wanted to have the keys but Susnjar wouldn't give him the keys. Milan wanted to lock those people up. He wanted to take them upstairs. Allegedly, he needed them for some kind of exchange. I don't know exactly what he had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did he actually say that? Did he actually tell you that he wanted to lock them up or that he wanted to take them for an exchange, or is it something that you were able to conclude from his behaviour?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: He wanted to lock those people up. He was asking for keys to the rooms, but Susnjar didn't want to give him the keys, which made him very rude, extremely rude, and he started making a lot of noise. Frankly speaking, I was very embarrassed because I was there with this senior colleague of mine with whom I had worked together for a very long time. But this didn't last very long, it all happened very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did Susnjar tell him why he didn't want to give him the keys? Was there any specific reason for that, or did they discuss the subject at all?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, it's -- well, it's hard for me to remember the details of the conversation. Actually, it was with Meho Dzafic that I went outside. I know that Susnjar didn't give him the keys most probably because he had been taking people there already. I don't know whether I can mention -- I mean, I've already said Susnjar. I think that he released some people that he had previously brought there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did anyone say something to that effect on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I cannot say that I personally heard that. It is possible that at that moment I was already outside with Meho. It's difficult for me to remember all of the details. What I do remember, however, is that he was very rude and that he insisted on having the keys and that Susnjar refused to give him the keys. He said he wanted to lock those people up and to later take them to be exchanged, because allegedly some Serbs had been taken prisoners and taken from Rujiste to Zepa. I don't know who. Who would know? I mean, all those plans that he had in mind, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So what happened when he didn't get the keys? What did Milan do at that point?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I left out -- I went out with Meho Dzafic and we talked for awhile, and Dzafic said, "I don't know what happened. He came to my house, he picked up some people." And then I said, "What does he want to do with you?" He told me that he wanted to have them exchanged. And I said, "Well, for whom are you supposed to be exchanged?" And he said he didn't know. He was very much afraid, and he said, "Mitar, could you please come with me, if you can," and I said, "Well, Meho, I will."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, would you please answer my questions. My question was: What did Milan do after those keys were not given to him?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: He said that they were to go back to the vehicles, to the cars, and that they were going to be exchanged. So I got out of the hotel with Meho --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So did they actually go there?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, I went out with Meho and Meho asked me if I had a cigarette. I gave him a cigarette, he smoked it halfway, and then Milan came and, rude as he was, he snatched that cigarette from him and he threw it away. He said, "You're not going to smoke in the car." And I said, "Well, why don't you let him finish his cigarette." And he said, "He's not going to smoke in the car," and then he said, "Now, get in the car." And I remember very well that I was sitting in the car -- Meho was sitting in the middle and I was sitting next to him, and there was another Muslim sitting to Meho's left. I was sitting on his right. There was also Meho's son with us, and the soldier under number 4 here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you left Vilina Vlas in a car?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Which car was the first one in line, in the column?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Lukic's car, a Passat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At one point in time you reached the junction at Sase. What happened next?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Some 500 metres from the junction, to the right, in the direction towards Prelovo, he stopped the car. In Sase, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did he leave the car? Did he get out of the car?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What about other passengers in his car?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes. We all got out of the car. Also, the people who were in the Jugo, they also got out of the car, pursuant to his orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And what happened next?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: He told us to continue down towards the Drina. Then at that point, people started panicking. The situation was not normal. And I said, "Milan, for God's sake, leave these people alone." He said, "I told you to go down to the Drina." So these people went down the meadow towards the Drina. Meho stayed with me. Meho was crying. And I remember Milan at one point in time putting his arm around Meho and I thought that he would have pity on him. And he said, "Mitar, would you please help me," and I said, "Milan, please, leave these people alone. What have they done to you? Nothing." And those other Muslims started to beg, but Milan wouldn't budge. He said, "No discussion. Just go down the meadow, continue towards the Drina." Those people were still begging him. There were people who couldn't swim. But he just wouldn't budge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Who said, "Who can swim?"

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Milan said. Milan did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: From what you have just told us, one can conclude that you too realised what the danger was, that you too could conclude that those people would be killed by Milan.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And that is indeed what happened, they were killed sometime later, except for the two individuals who managed to save themselves?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you think that you were in a position to prevent that?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I was trying. I begged him, but it was impossible to order him to do anything or to ask him anything. He was -- he was cruel. He wouldn't listen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you went down towards the Drina with those people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: How far did you go with them? How far did you accompany them; all the way down, or did you stop at one point?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I stopped some 10 or 15 metres before the river, because I realised that there was nothing that can be done, that it was all over.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did Milan or someone else line up those people on the bank of the river?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, they went all the way down to the river. I remained where I was, some 10 or 15 metres away from the bank, near some bushes. I could hear the noise, I could hear people cry and beg, but it was to no avail. And then shooting started and I heard those shots and I heard those terrible moans, screams of people being drowned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: How many of them opened fire? How many of them actually shot?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Three of them. Three of them actually went down to the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Are you also counting Milan Lukic amongst those three individuals?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were you behind those people at the moment the shooting started?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: How far were you, and where exactly where you standing?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I was some 10 to 15 metres away from them, actually, away from the water.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At the spot where you were, were there any bushes or trees?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: There were some bushes, some brambles growing near the water.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you tell us what kind of bushes those were?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, it's the kind of -- it's a kind of bush or a tree which grows near the water. Usually you would find such bushes and small trees growing near rivers. And there were also some other trees there, some poplars, the kind of trees that you usually find near the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you remained there, near those trees, and you were some 10 or 15 metres behind the people, behind the individuals who shot at the group which was standing at the bank of the river; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you watch the shooting itself?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, not directly. I didn't watch them kill those people. I turned around because it was very difficult for me to watch that. But I could hear the shots and I could hear people getting drowned. It was terrible to listen to all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you ever -- were you ever present at any shooting incident before that?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No, never. I had never seen any shooting except in the movies. Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And what happened next?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: They shot those people dead. I started up the meadow; they followed. And, What did you do? Why did you have to do that? But he wouldn't turn a hair. He just didn't care, that's how he behaved. So we reached the vehicles. We set off. I got out at my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mean your house at the entrance into Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And who were you in the car with?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So in the same car that you went to the Drina; is that it?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you discuss the things that you saw that day with anyone?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: It was difficult to do that. I was very distraught even before that, and it was -- it was very hard for me. I tried to. I was washing my face, I poured water on the back of my neck. Everything that happened, it was just too hard to even think about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But what did you tell your wife? Did you tell her the whole story?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I told her. I told her how Milan had brought Meho and his son and another five and how he killed them next to the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you talk about this with anyone else?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: In the morning, I went to the police station and I told the commander, Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Why him?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Why, he was the commander, and I knew him too. He came from the neighbourhood and he was the police chief, so who else would I go to?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did Tomic say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: He asked me what was that, what happened, who were those men. He wrote it down, the cause for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know if he took any steps?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I don't. I don't know if he took any steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you about -- something about what you did when you were a street-sweep.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, I told Stanko the same thing. Stanko wanted to banish him from Visegrad, but then Stanko got killed too so that -- well, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Will you tell me something about what you did when you tried to clean the town up. You said that you organised the sweeping of streets. Now, how, where, what did you do, and who helped you in that?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: The town was really in shambles, very unkempt, and so at Bikavac, in the command, they suggested to me to organise the cleaning up of the town. "Would you do that?" "Sure," I said. "Who did this?" "Well, those were salesmen or businessmen." Everybody did in front of their buildings, or tenants in front of their buildings, postmen in front of the post office, in the neighbourhood -- in different neighbourhoods, I mean, where individual houses stand, it was usually the housewives. And we worked until 9.00 or 10.00 so that the town was put back in order. It had never been cleaner than then. Never. Everybody did his bit and everything was put in order, cleaned and swept. You couldn't recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say 9.00 or 10.00, that means one hour a day; is that it?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you do it daily, or did it depend on something else?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, usually, yes. In front of the shops, restaurants, selling outlets, post offices, banks, newsstands, usually at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you organised these drives, what did you wear; civilian or some other clothes?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, everything. I mean, civilian clothes. I also wore that old SMB, the olive-green/grey uniform. At times I would have the army trousers and a civilian shirt. I mean, there was no obligation, one didn't have to wear anything special, nor did I have any clothes that would show what I was doing. The only thing I had was this red ribbon. And those people, I mean, the Visegradians, they knew me. And they did that, they liked to do that, especially in front of their shops and businesses. You didn't have to say anything to them, those people, especially saleswomen, they all swept it clean.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And on such occasions, did you always wear that red ribbon?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes. I think we were the busiest in my street, because when the lake was released, of course, the water had carried all sorts of things, poplar trunks and branches and all that, and so we had to bring some saws to -- some electric saws to do that, but of course it was the men who did that because it was all brought in by the water, but we managed to clean that up too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did both the Serbs and Muslims take part in that?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, yes, people from the buildings. Yes, everybody. Everybody who lived in the residential buildings, they would come down and do that. Nobody was forced to do that. There were no summons issued to people to come out to that. No, never. And besides, I had no right to do any such thing. Nobody was forced to do that. People accepted to do that, and the town was clean as clean, and we helped. We also helped the public utilities company. We tried to put all the rubbish in some parcels, and then a truck would come and we would just load it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: These drives, did they go on until that day when you suffered you injury or, rather, when you broke your leg?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Until up to that day, you mean, that day?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I mean the period preceding it and that day.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, the preceding period, all the time up to that day and on that day too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And that day, that is, the last day, the day when you suffered your injury, did you happen on Pionirska Street?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you recall how sometime, somewhere near the elementary school on Pionirska Street, how you walked down the street, inviting people to come out and clean the streets? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I went everywhere; to Bikavac and Pionirska Street, and Jondza, and Kalate, and the area towards the station. I did rounds of all that. And people did it. I asked people and they did it. I mean, really, everybody, whoever had time, and everybody was keen to do it, and people were very happy because the town was suddenly all clean. I mean, it was so unkempt and it looked in such disorder and there was so much dirt around and waste paper and posters and all that, it was all over the place, but that was all removed, taken away. You couldn't recognise it. All the broken glass, all the shards, we all took that out, collected it, removed it, everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Fine. You have explained it to us all in detail, and I think that is clear now. But what I asked you was whether you remembered how, on that day, you were on Pionirska Street, somewhere near the elementary school, that is, in the upper part of the street, and as you walked down the street, how you invited people to come out and sweep the streets. And do you remember if you had a loudspeaker of any kind or something, a loudspeaker?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Leading, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. By the way, on the previous one, both you and I, I think, probably missed, but about three questions before you took your previous objection, the witness had in fact referred to those. I was distracted because Mr. Domazet had actually remonstrated with his client to answer his question, so I didn't really take much notice of the answer he had given but it had been given there. But this one, Mr. Domazet, whereabouts has the witness given evidence about this? You opened it, but about the last three questions, if I may suggest to you, are suggesting to him the answer. One of the worst of them was, "Did you just happen upon Pionirska Street?" Now, do you suggest that he has given this evidence about the loudspeaker?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a witness mentioned that loudspeaker and he claimed that, on that occasion, Mr. Vasiljevic had one such loudspeaker in his hands, and that is why I -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, that is still a leading question. Now, please let the witness give the evidence. Don't give it from the bar table. If you want us to place weight upon his evidence, please do not lead him. Now, that's very basic. You are destroying your own client's evidence by leading him along these lines. I know the witness gave evidence about it, but that's not the point here. You ask him what he recalls having been said. If he is unable to do it, then you can draw his attention to the evidence which the witness has given as such. But that was clearly leading. But the worst of them, and I wondered why there was no objection, was that expression, "You just happened to be on Pionirska Street." Now, please, that's a very vital issue in this case, so help your client by not leading him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. I will then withdraw this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So, Mr. Vasiljevic, my question is: What do you remember about Pionirska Street on that day; that is, what did you do there? Did you have anything in your hands? How were you dressed?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: To be quite honest, I am charged with that crime on Pionirska Street, but I never knew about that crime until I arrived in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just a moment. We may arrive there, but I'm asking you to give me specific answers to my questions. My question was whether you remember what you wore on that occasion, did you have anything in your hands, and where were you headed when you found yourself on Pionirska Street?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I had the SMB trousers, a shirt - it was of a dark colour because it was after my cousin's death I told you about - boots, and a bottle, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And did you have anything on your head?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, now, Mr. Domazet, at that stage you are entitled to ask him specifically about the witness's evidence as to what he had in his hands and what he had on his head. You can ask him specifically now in relation to that evidence. You've got him to exhaust his recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So, Mr. Vasiljevic, apart from the bottle which you mentioned, do you recall that you had anything else in your hands?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No, I don't recall anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm speaking about that bottle. What is that? Was it a full Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. bottle or, rather, what was there in the bottle, if there was anything?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, alcohol, what else? Brandy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were you drinking then from that bottle?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, I must have, surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And on Pionirska Street, did you then come across a person whom you had known from before?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes. I came across (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, I don't know if you misunderstood me, but you are now entitled to put to him the evidence which the witnesses have given to enable him to deny them if it be the case. For example, if he was wearing a big floppy black hat, was he wearing one? I don't want you to have misunderstood what I have said. You have to get him, first of all, to give his version before you can put the witness's evidence to him, but now you've taken him through it, he says he has no recollection, you can say to him, Were you wearing a big, black, floppy hat? if I've got the right description, and you can put to him what the witnesses said he had in his hand and he is then able to deny it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, you said that now and then you would wear a black hat, but you could not remember that you had any head covering on that occasion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, I did have a black hat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And that black hat was a broad-rimmed hat, or how was it?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No, no, no, it was a military hat with upturned brim.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So it was a narrow-brimmed hat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you ever wear a straw hat?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No, never. It's yellow. A straw hat is yellow.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Or perhaps a hat of any other colour except that black hat that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No. That was the only one that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In addition to what you have just described, did you have a coat?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I never wore any coat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You say you never wore any coat. So on that occasion or any other occasion, you simply do not wear any coats?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No, I've never worn a long coat in my life. Had I had one, I wouldn't have been soaked by the rain. I never wore that, never in my life. I never had one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And did you have any weapon on you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And did you have a megaphone or some loudspeaker or some PA device?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you use any such contraption to call people, to summon people, or did you use only your own unaided voice?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Only the first day, only when this drive started, when I started organising this, that was the only time I did that. After that, no, there was no need to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I understand that once, in the beginning, you used a loudspeaker.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes. After that, people knew about that. There was no need to organise people any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Are you sure, or would you allow that you perhaps did have a loudspeaker with you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No, no, no, I was off on another -- on a different errand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And that was?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I went to get a horse from a settlement called Vucina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And is that the road to Vucina, you take Pionirska Street to go there?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Awhile ago you said that you had noticed and approached your acquaintance, (redacted).

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Will you tell me something about that conversation that you had, if, that is, you had any?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I knew Mujo well. He came from the village of Sase, and he'd pass by my house every day when he worked -- when he went to work. And he also frequented various restaurants and coffee bars, especially coffee bars. He was quite fond of drink too. So we inquired after each other's health. "So what's new, Mujo?" and he said, "Well, nothing. We have to go." He says, "We've just received orders to go to Kladanj." "Why is that? What's that?" And I know that he told me that his wife had left already. Well, we had a drink and he offered also his cows to me. He said, "I've got two cows. Want them?" "What do I want these cows for, Mujo? You know I have nowhere to keep them. I have no use for them," I said. And so we talked for awhile, and I said, "Well, don't worry, boy, you'll be back. All this madness will pass." "Oh, well, I don't know what to do." Well, it was nine years ago. I don't really remember all that we talked about, but that was that, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember anything else that was said in that conversation, or do you remember anything that you think would be important to tell us?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: There was Mujo's neighbour with him. I don't know what his name is, but he was building a house next to Mujo, on his left, about 200 metres down below the road. Mujo lived in Jasarevici, and this man -- you know, where that warehouse is. They're neighbours. As a matter of fact, that house wasn't finished yet but he was building it, I know that, passing by my place. What his name is, I don't know. I knew him by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did (redacted) know about your cleaning drives, rather, that you headed those actions?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I'm sure he didn't because I didn't go down to villages. But he -- perhaps he did ask me because of the ribbon or something. I may have said something. But what I'm not sure about I won't talk about, because the crime is a very severe crime, so I won't talk about that. And it's a long time ago, and I wouldn't have remembered any of this had it not been for (redacted) there, nor would I have remembered any of the other people because I just passed by them. I don't know what to say. I'm being accused of having done this, so to give you every detail about everything that we talked about, I really can't remember it all. We might have spent some half an hour together, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you -- and you were drinking brandy all that while with him?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You say that you don't really remember it all because you never thought that it might become important. But did you pay any attention to other persons who were possibly around there, or is it that you don't remember any such thing?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I know that he told me that they were ordered to leave, to go. There were quite a few people there, including women. I remember the weather. It was cloudy and the wind was blowing. I was also in a hurry. I wanted to fetch that horse. But I would have stayed with him for awhile, I'm sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Apart from that conversation that you had with him, tete-a-tete for about half an hour, did you personally address anyone else? Did you say anything to anyone, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No. It wasn't possible for me to address them in any way. I didn't know who was behind it, who was in charge of the overall organisation. There was nothing I could have possibly told those people. Nor did I know that they were heading somewhere. I don't know who -- I didn't know who was in charge, who took the initiative to take them wherever they were being taken to. I really didn't know anything. I must have told them something, if anyone asked me anything, but I wasn't organising anything. I never escorted any such group. I had no idea about such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I was just about to ask you, Mr. Vasiljevic, if you had heard, if you had become aware before your conversation with Meho, that any such group had left Visegrad, or was it at that time that you learned about that?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No, I never knew anything about that. I had no idea that they would have to leave Koritnik and be taken somewhere. I really didn't know who was the organiser. I would have passed by and continued on my way if I had not seen Mujo. But because I knew Mujo, I just wondered and I stopped, and then he was telling me all these things and I felt really sorry for him. We had had a drink on a number of occasions before that, so I offered him to drink on that occasion as well, and I said that we would see each other soon again or something like that. But now you're asking me about specific things and who was in charge of the organisation of all -- I mean, I really don't know. Who was I, after all? I wasn't issuing any tasks, any duties to anyone. They had been sent by the Red Cross to the Pionirska Street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, you really must pause before you start your answer. You're coming in far too quickly. So pause a bit longer, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, this is one of the problems when you're having something translated; I may have interrupted his answer there. I thought he'd finished. You may want to pick up about the Red Cross there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that's what I was about to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: How do you know that, Mr. Vasiljevic? How do you know that they were sent by the Red Cross to go to Pionirska Street?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Mujo told me that. He told me that they had been given orders to that effect, and he said that they were running late on that day and that -- yes, and I also remember that he told me that his wife had already left. That, I remember. But it's all blurred in my mind. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, did you personally ever work for the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you ever introduce yourself as an employee of the Red Cross to anyone?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No. How could I? I didn't dare. I mean, why would I have done such a thing? Why would I have falsely introduced myself? I would have, I don't know, had to know something about the work itself and how it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: On that occasion while you were with (redacted), did he or anyone else ask you to write something down for them?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No. I couldn't write anything down for him. I could have perhaps given him my address or a telephone number, but no, no. What could I have possibly written to him? I was just nobody, and he knew that. And I -- I was working at that time, but I was not dressed in a fancy manner, as an official of some kind. I didn't look like anyone in an official capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, could you answer my questions. Is your answer no?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you carry a piece of paper or a pencil with you?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No, no, I had no paper whatsoever. It was -- it wasn't possible for me to give them any such piece of paper, because such a piece of paper would have had to have a seal, a stamp of some kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, please concentrate yourself on my questions. Did you have any paper, any pencil or pen with you on that occasion? Did you have it on you?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No, no. How could I have? I cannot even remember that I had a piece of paper or a pencil. I may have had it, but I don't know. I didn't need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: After you left (redacted), did you continue on your way? Did you go and fetch that horse?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, I went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: On the way back, did you again see (redacted) or anyone else, if you took the same street on the way back?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, I went back along the same street. I didn't see Mujo. I don't remember seeing anyone else. But I remember that I did not see Mujo, that's for sure. And it was going to rain. I was riding that horse, and at the moment I was leaving the town, when I was in the outskirts of the town, I remembered that it began to rain and it was actually quite a shower which struck suddenly. And I remember that -- I remember the sun rays coming through the clouds. I remember that particular moment because it was at that time that I fell off the horse.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you were riding a horse along Pionirska Street and you were going towards the centre of the town. Does that mean that you were riding in the direction of the Visegrad Hotel?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember how fast you were riding? Slowly or quickly? What was your speed?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't riding very fast. The horse did not have a saddle on, and the horse didn't have horseshoes on, and that was perhaps one of the reasons why it tripped, and also because the surface of the street was slippery.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: How did you fall?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, at the moment, I was near the -- near a restaurant, I wanted to take the horse to the railway because I was afraid that somebody would take it. It's difficult for me to explain. It was Semso who called me from the terrace, and this Professor Mitrovic was there. I must have turned around. Maybe it was my fault that the horse fell down, that it tripped. But whatever happened, the horse tripped and it fell down, and I fell, of course, with the horse and I fell on my left leg and it hurt immediately. The horse immediately stood up and I wasn't able to get off the ground because my leg was hurting me very badly. And then Pero and this other guy approached me, and I remember that it was raining. It was no longer a shower but it was still drizzling. And then Pero took my leg, he felt it, and he said, "I think you've broken it."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphones are off.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: So since I was unable to get up, they called the ambulance from the hotel. I spent some 10 or 15 minutes lying there, and then the ambulance arrived. They put me on a stretcher and they took me in to the ambulance which drove me to the hospital in Visegrad. Let me just say that it was Zivorad Savic who drove the car. I know him. Once in hospital, I was admitted by a physician who was there. His name is Goran Loncarevic. They took me to the x-ray machine, and the doctor said, "Mitar, you have broken two bones." And they put the sling on my leg with some extension weights, and I was no longer in pain. Of course, when I tried to move the leg, it hurt, but as long as I was still, I was okay, it wasn't painful. I stayed there for awhile. I waited for some time, and I think that in the meantime the ambulance left. They were off to see a patient in his house. The doctor provided me with the necessary documentation, including his opinion and recommendations, whatever I might need for this other hospital, and he sent me to the hospital in Uzice. I am not able to tell you the exact time, what time it was when we left Visegrad. Whether it was 7.00 or 8.00, I don't know. I remember it was still raining, it was still cloudy, and me and the driver left the hospital. As we were passing by the Sarajevo bank, a building in the centre of the town, Mile Novakovic was there, he lived in the vicinity, and he was head of the accountancy service of that bank. And that is how we started for Uzice. As we were passing through the village of Vardiste, I asked the driver to stop by the house of my uncle and to bring me a blanket because I was getting cold.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, you have now told us that story on your own, without any questions. I do not wish to repeat anything, but I would just like to know whether that was the uncle who had this coffee shop in Vardiste and whose son was killed and whose burial you attended. Is that the uncle you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So it was your uncle who gave you this blanket for you to cover yourself. Apart from that, did the driver and this person by the name of Novakovic who was with you stay at the coffee shop?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: The two of them went to the cafe and stayed there for awhile. They had a coffee there or a drink, I don't know. And they brought me some juice. My uncle and my aunt came down to see me and they asked me what had happened, "You've broken your leg," and I said yes. "So you have to go to hospital now?" and I said yes. Then the driver came back together with Mile Novakovic and we continued our journey towards Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Before that, Mr. Vasiljevic, I would like to know whether you received any medication at the medical centre in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know why?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Well, they couldn't give me any medicine because of all the alcohol that I had drunk that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you inform your family or wife of what had happened to you?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: When I came to Vardiste, actually, it was my uncle who gave her a call because I told him to inform her.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So it was from him that she learned that you were on your way to Uzice and that you had been injured?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, she told me that he was the one who informed her first about what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were there any checkpoints on that road, and did you have to stop?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes. There was a checkpoint on the Bosnian side and then another one on the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember what time it was when you reached the Uzice hospital, approximately?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you the exact hour. I mean, I can tell you what I can find in the documents. The document says 2135, but it could have been some ten minutes earlier than that. But it was at that time, more or less. At least, that's what was recorded by the woman who was at the reception. So it was around that time that I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was it already dark?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At the time you left Visegrad, was it still daylight?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Once at the hospital in Uzice, were any additional x-rays taken? Were you examined? What happened?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: They took some x-rays of my leg again. Again, they diagnosed a fracture. I remember that I was admitted by Dr. Dusko Jovicic in that hospital, whom I had not known prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you know anyone else?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: He was assisted by his colleague, Alexandar Moljevic, whom I knew very well. He is from Visegrad by origin and he used to work as a GP in Visegrad for several years. Later on, he specialised in something. I don't know exactly where he was for his specialisation. I know that he ended up working in Uzice, and he was the one on duty that night together with Jovicic. But my lead doctor was Dr. Jovicic. He was the one who followed me, because normally it is the doctor who initially admits you that is also in charge for further observation of the patient. Anyway, so they took off the bandages that were applied in Visegrad, and I think they put them back again. The following morning, they took blood from me and carried out all the necessary examinations, the usual one which is done on admittance to hospital. Then he said that I was to undergo a surgery, and I thought -- I didn't know what they were going to do. I was afraid that they might amputate my leg. And then he said, no, no, no, we're just going to drill it a little bit. So they took me away together with the bed which had wheels on, and they took me to a surgery theatre. There was a woman patient before me, I remember, and some drilling surgery was performed on her as well. And I heard her scream and I thought that it was a very painful procedure. So when she was finished, it was my turn. They applied some ointment on my heel and they took this drill and --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, I don't think that we need all of these details. They are not crucial to the case. So you were admitted to the hospital, and on the following morning you underwent surgery.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, they performed some minor drilling surgery on my heel. It was not a very complex operation. They just needed to make a little hole in my heel so that those extension weights could be applied on my leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What was the purpose, what was the objective of that surgery?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: They needed to stretch my muscles so that the bones would heel properly. I don't know exactly why they did it or what the reason was, but anyway, that is what I was told. Anyway, when I was back to my room, I was lying on my bed, underneath some extensions with some weights on it, and I had to spend 21 days lying like that. I mean, that was the usual procedure that was applied in cases like mine, and it lasted at least 20 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does it mean that you were bedridden for 21 days with the extensions applied to your leg, together with the weights, and is it correct that you were not able to leave your bed because of that?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It is impossible to leave the bed, because those weights are applied to my -- to my leg through this hole that they had drilled in my heel. It was only possible for me to sit on the bed but not to leave the bed altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember the room where you were? Did it have several beds? Were you there together with other patients?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: There were four of us altogether. My bed was the one next to the window. There was an elderly gentleman from Uzice, then a Muslim who was from Gorazde who had had his leg amputated, and then another man from Uzice whose bed was next to this Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you spent three weeks in that department, orthopaedic department.

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And after that?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: After that, I was transferred to the neuropsychiatric ward within the same hospital. I mean, it was part of the same hospital complex but Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in a different building.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What was the reason for that transfer, Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I was in a very difficult state, psychologically and emotionally. I had those visions and fears. I was imagining all kinds of things, that I was talking to God, to the devil. There were all kinds of strange visions and images that came to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you have any problems, any quarrels with the staff of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: I think I did. I don't remember the details, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet --

utterances.speaker: Mitar Vasiljevic
utterances.text: But I had -- it was a very strange period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: -- what do you think is left in your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't have that many questions left, but I think I can also finish for today and then continue on Thursday, because there was -- I just wanted to use the day of tomorrow to recover a little bit. I am somewhat under the weather and I don't feel very well. However, if Your Honour thinks that it is important for me to continue and see this examination-in-chief to its end, I can try and do my best and finish today, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Not at all, Mr. Domazet. It was in response to an inquiry you made, as I understood it, of one of the legal officers that you wanted to have a consultation with your client tomorrow, and I pointed out to you that if you could fit that in between the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination, the Trial Chamber would listen sympathetically to your application. But if you are, indeed, in need of a recovery, you probably won't be going out to see your client anyway. I certainly don't want you to pursue the case at this stage if you are not up to it, and if you are not in need or you are not able to interview your client tomorrow. So we will continue on Thursday morning. It's a matter for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. Then we'll adjourn now and we'll resume at 9.30 on Thursday. Have a very happy United Nations holiday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 25th day of October, 2001, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.05 p.m.,
